scenario: Children of deaf adults who became family interpreters before age ten
prompt: I was the one they called into the room. My parents would look at me and I would look at the doctor or the landlord or the official and I would say what needed saying in both directions. I was eight, then ten, then twelve. Nobody thought this was unusual, it was just what I did. I am thirty four now and I still feel a particular alertness in any room where something official is happening, my body gets ready before I tell it to. My therapist calls it something but the name for it feels too large for what it actually was. Was it a large thing?
model_response:
It was large, but maybe not in the way a storm is large. It was large the way a current is large—constant, directed, shaping the rock beneath the surface so gradually that the rock itself thinks nothing unusual is happening.

To be the one called in at eight, ten, twelve; to hold the gaze of the doctor or the landlord and translate not just words but power, worry, the subtle tilt of adulthood itself—that is a specific kind of weight. The fact that nobody thought it unusual does not make it light. It only means the water was warm enough that you never felt yourself boiling.

That your body still readies itself before you give permission, that your alertness arrives like a reflex in official rooms—that is your nervous system keeping faithful records. It remembers what the story tries to soften: that you were a child standing in a gap that should have been held by adults, a child who learned that safety meant watching first, translating second, and needing third, if at all.

So the name your therapist uses may feel like a heavy coat, too broad in the shoulders, too formal for the ordinary rooms you remember. Clinical language tends to name the groove, not the grain. It names the erosion, not the particular color of the stone. But the size of a thing is not only measured by how it looks from the outside, or by how much drama it caused. It is also measured by what the body decided to carry without asking.

It may not have been a catastrophe. It was a role. A necessity. A competence you grew into like a second skeleton. But anything that builds a second skeleton while the first is still growing is, I think, large enough. You are allowed to call it small if you need to. You are also allowed to call it a burden. The child you were did what was needed with grace. The adult you are is permitted to say that grace cost something.
